The intelligentsia is a group of people within a society who are recognized as its intellectual and cultural elite. These are highly educated individuals who make it their business — or their deep passion — to think seriously about the world. They engage with big ideas in fields like philosophy, literature, art, science, politics, and culture. More than just being educated, they actively use their minds to analyze, question, interpret, and shape the way society thinks about itself.

Think of them as the "thinking class" of a society.
Who exactly counts as the intelligentsia?

Professors, writers, poets, philosophers, journalists, artists, scientists, scholars, and intellectuals broadly. The common thread is not just their education, but what they do with it — they produce, debate, and spread ideas. A university professor who writes books challenging political systems is part of the intelligentsia. A poet who writes verse that forces people to see the world differently is part of the intelligentsia. A scientist who publicly engages with ethical questions about humanity belongs there too.

However — and this is important — simply having a college degree does not make someone part of the intelligentsia. A trained accountant or an engineer doing routine technical work, regardless of how qualified they are, would not typically be called part of the intelligentsia. The defining quality is active, critical intellectual engagement with ideas that matter to society.

The intelligentsia serves as a society's conscience, critic, and cultural compass. They are the people who ask the difficult questions: Is our government just? What does this art say about us? What are the moral consequences of this new technology? Where is our civilization heading? They write the books, compose the essays, deliver the lectures, and spark the debates that shape how ordinary people come to understand the world around them.

In this sense, they hold real influence — not political power in the direct sense, but the softer, deeper power of shaping ideas, values, and culture. Governments throughout history have recognized this power, which is exactly why authoritarian regimes have historically feared, censored, exiled, or imprisoned members of the intelligentsia.
How the word is used — and its tone

The word can be used with admiration, neutrality, or even mild contempt, depending on the speaker and context.

Used admirably, it recognizes a society's brightest and most thoughtful minds — the people who keep civilization intellectually alive and progressing.

Used neutrally, it simply describes this social class without any special praise or criticism — for example, "The intelligentsia played a major role in shaping public opinion during the revolution."

Used with a slightly critical or ironic edge, it can imply that these people are out of touch with ordinary life — too absorbed in abstract ideas, too elite, too self-important, or disconnected from the struggles of working people. Someone might say, dismissively, "Oh, the intelligentsia are debating this endlessly in their academic journals while the rest of us have real problems." This critical use reflects a long-standing tension between intellectual elites and the general population.

So the word carries no permanently fixed emotional charge — context and tone decide it.

Intelligentsia is always a collective noun — it refers to the group as a whole, never to a single person. You would never call one brilliant professor "an intelligentsia." Instead, you would say that person is "a member of the intelligentsia" or "part of the intelligentsia." This is similar to how you'd say someone is "a member of the clergy" rather than calling them "a clergy."

The word has no common singular form and is not typically pluralized (you would not say "intelligentsias"). It stands as one solid, collective term for the intellectual class as a unit.

If someone says "the intelligentsia of 19th-century Russia," they mean the educated, thinking class of that time and place — the writers, philosophers, and political thinkers who were debating ideas about freedom, justice, and society. If someone says "the Western intelligentsia has largely ignored this issue," they mean that educated intellectual circles in the West have been paying too little attention to it. If a novelist is described as "beloved by the intelligentsia," it means intellectuals and literary circles hold that novelist in high regard — though, depending on context, it might also subtly hint that the writer's appeal is limited to elite, educated readers rather than the general public.

In short: the intelligentsia is the educated intellectual class of a society — the thinkers, creators, and critics who engage deeply with ideas and whose work shapes the culture and thought of their time.
